slides.text:
A regular expression is a pattern that describes a family of texts: every ticket id, every date, every number in a log. The `regexp` package finds, extracts and rewrites them.

The pattern `\d+` means one or more digits.

Go's engine always runs in linear time, so no pattern can hang the program. The price is that it has no lookahead and no backreferences.

Compile a pattern once and reuse it. Compiling inside a loop wastes time.
You will match texts, find and extract them, then capture groups and replace text.

A pattern is made of pieces. Some match one character:

- `.` any character
- `\d` a digit
- `\w` a letter, digit or `_`
- `\s` a space or a tab
- `[A-Z]` one from a set

Quantifiers say how many times, and anchors pin the position:

- `+` one or more
- `*` zero or more
- `?` zero or one
- `{3}` exactly three
- `^` and `$` the start and the end of the text

Without anchors a pattern matches anywhere in the text. Characters like `.`, `+`, `(` and `[` have a meaning, so a literal dot is written `\.`.

A backtick string is raw, so `\d` needs no doubling.

slides.text: The find methods are built from the same words. This is pseudo code for how the names grow, not Go.
slides.code:
Find        the first match
FindAll     every match
...String   works on a string
...Index    positions, not text
...Submatch also the groups

slides.text:
No match is not an error: `FindString` returns an empty string, and the slice versions return `nil`.

`FindAllString(text, n)` stops after `n` matches, and `-1` means all of them.

exercises.title: Limits
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
re := regexp.MustCompile(`[a-z]+`)
text := "ab cd ef"
fmt.Println(
    re.FindAllString(text, 2),
    re.FindAllString(text, 0),
)
exercises.explanation: A limit of 2 stops after two matches. A limit of 0 asks for none, so the result is an empty slice.

slides.text: Parentheses capture part of a match as a group. A submatch result lists the whole match first, then each group in order of its opening parenthesis. This is pseudo code.

A group can have a name, `(?P<name>...)`, so you do not count positions.

Groups also feed the replacement: in the new text, `$1` stands for the first group of each match.

exercises.title: Group names
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
re := regexp.MustCompile(`(\d+)kg`)
a := re.ReplaceAllString("5kg", "$1g")
b := re.ReplaceAllString("5kg", "${1}g")
fmt.Printf("%q %q\n", a, b)
exercises.explanation: `$1g` is read as a group named `1g`, which does not exist, so it adds nothing. Braces end the name: `${1}g` is group 1 and then `g`.

slides.text: `MustCompile` panics on a broken pattern, which is fine for a pattern you wrote in your code. A pattern that comes from outside needs `Compile`, which returns an error to check.
To match text from a user literally, wrap it with `QuoteMeta`: it escapes every character that has a meaning in a pattern.

`+` and `*` are greedy: they take as much text as they can. Adding `?` makes them lazy, taking as little as possible.

The difference shows when the text around the match can repeat.

exercises.title: Why QuoteMeta?
exercises.guide: Pick what the call to `QuoteMeta` is for.
options: Checks the pattern for syntax errors
Makes the match ignore letter case
Matches the name literally, dot included
Turns the name into capture groups
exercises.explanation: `QuoteMeta` escapes characters like `.` so they match themselves. Without it, `a.b` would also match `axb`.
